The bridge was not grand in the way of cathedrals, yet it had a kind of patience that made people trust it. Its timbers had been seasoned by many seasons, and its ropes had learned the language of wind. Each evening, the lanterns were lit one by one along its rails, small flames cupped in glass, trembling as if uncertain whether they were meant to guide or merely to keep company with the dark.

Rain came first as a whisper against the valley. It touched the leaves of the alders and made them shine. Then it gathered itself into threads, then into curtains, until the whole crossing seemed suspended in a silver hush. The water below, swollen and restless, carried the reflections of the lanterns in broken pieces. Each ripple turned the light into a moving creature, gold and green and sometimes almost violet, as though the night were trying on different faces.

Travelers who crossed there often spoke of the bridge as if it were a threshold. On one side lay the familiar world of fields and hearths; on the other, the unknown country of roads and promises. The rain made that feeling stronger. It blurred the edges of things. A farmer returning with his cart would pause at the center, listening to the drumming on his oilskin, and for a moment he would not think of home or debt or weather, but only of the strange beauty that can appear when the world is washed clean.

The lanterns did not fight the rain so much as translate it. Where the drops struck the glass, they scattered the glow into tiny stars.
